Next we have the reliability, which is being shown here as 255 out of 255. This means if the connection begins to have more inputs or output errors, you're going to see the reliability lower. The next two lines are the last input, last output, and last clearing of the counters. In this case, the router was just rebooted, so they're all set to zero because they were all just cleared. Basically, when the router or switch has to say it needs to start shedding some load and it starts dropping packets selectively, SPD is a protocol that's going to drop your lowest priority packets when the CPU becomes too busy, so that way it can save capacity for higher priority packets as a form of quality of service. Now, the total output drops here is at zero. This means that we've had no drops because we never had a full output queue. Since we have 100 megabit per second connection, as long as we're communicating with another 100 megabit per second connection, we should see this stay at zero drop packets. If we started using a 20 megabit per second connection, for instance on our ISP, then we might likely have an experience here with network congestion because we're sending it 100, but they can only take it at 20. That would cause a problem for us, and at that point, some of our packets might get dropped. Next, we have our queuing strategy for our quality of service. In this case, we're setting this as first in, first out, which is known as FIFO. This is the default for this type of router. Next, we have output queue size and the maximum. Currently, our queue is empty and it's showing zero packets. Now the maximum queue size here is set at 40, so if I receive more than 40 packets, the queue is not going to be able to hold it and the rest of those will get dropped. Next, we have our minute input and output rates. Now here are the average rates at which packets are being received and being transmitted. Now, a runt is an ethernet frame that is less than 64 bytes in size. It's really small, that's why it's a runt. A giant is any ethernet frame that exceeds the 802.3 frame size of 1,518 bytes. It's really large, so it's a giant. Throttles are going to occur when the interface fails to buffer the incoming packets. If this is a high number, this is an indicator that you may be having quality of service issues to your end users. Next, we have input errors, CRC, frame overrun and ignored. The input error counter will go up whenever the interface is receiving a frame with any kind of error in it. This can be something like a runt, a giant, no buffer available, CRC errors or other things like that. CRC is the number of packets that were received but failed the cyclic redundancy checksum or CRC check upon receiving them. If the checksum generated by the sender doesn't match the one calculated by this interface, when it receives that frame, a CRC error is counted and the packet gets rejected. Now, frame is used to count the number of packets where a CRC error and a non integer number of octets was received. Overrun is used to count how often the interface was unable to receive traffic due to an insufficient hardware buffer. Ignored is going to be used to count the number of packets that the interface ignored since the hardware interface was low on the internal buffers. If you're experiencing a lot of noise on the connection or broadcast storm, this ignored count will start to rise drastically. Next, we have the watchdog counter, which is used to count how many times the watchdog timer has expired. This happens whenever a packet over 2048 bytes is received. The next line contains the input packets with dribble condition detected, which means that a slightly longer than default frame was received by the interface. For example, we talked about the fact that the MTU size was 1500 bytes by default, but a frame wasn't considered a giant until it reached 1,518 bytes. So if I got a frame that was 1,510 bytes inside, it's technically above the MTU size, but it's not yet a giant, so it would still be processed, but it would be added here on the dribble condition counter so I can know that I'm starting to get packets above 1500 bytes. Next, we have the output errors, and this is just like our input errors. The only difference is we're now counting the number of collisions and the interface resets that are occurring as a result. Next, we have the interface reset, and this the number of times an interface had to be completely reset since the last reboot. Next, we have unknown protocol drops. Anytime a protocol drops, but our device can't determine what protocol it was, it's going to be listed under the unknown protocol drops. For example, if you're not supposed to receive older types of protocols like IPX traffic and Apple Talk on your router, but somebody sends you a message that's formatted that way, your router's going to drop it and it's not going to know what it was because it's not a properly formatted IP message or an ethernet frame, so that counter is going to go up. Next, we have babbles, late collision and deferred. Now, a babble is used to count any frame that is transmitted that is larger than 1,518 bytes. This is similar to our giants, but we're going to use this when we're transmitting instead of receiving, a babble is for transmission, a giant is for receipt. Late collisions are going to be used to count the number of collisions that occur after the interface started transmitting its frame and deferred is used to count the number of frames that were transmitted successfully after waiting because the media was busy. So if your devices are using CSMA/CD or collision detection, it's going to detect the media is busy. It's going to wait, and then it's going to transmit. When this happens, this number's going to go up because it had to wait. Again, we should see zero for late collisions and deferred here because we're using a full duplex connection, but if we're using a half duplex connection, there will be some numbers there. Next, we have the lost carrier and the no carrier. This is the number of times that the carrier was lost or not present during the transmission. The carrier we're talking about here is the signal on the connection. Finally, we have the output buffer failures and swapped out, the output buffer failure is going to be used to count the number of times a packet was not output from the output hold queue because of a shortage of shared memory. An output buffer swap out is going to be the number of packets stored in the main memory when the queue was full. If this number is very high, that means that you're likely experiencing a busy time in your networks. Now, for the exam, you don't need to know all of these things and memorize all their definitions, but you should be aware of some key statistics here on the interface. Things like the link state, the speed and duplex status, the send and receive traffic statistics, the cyclic redundancy check statistics, the protocol packet and byte counts, the CRC errors, the giants, the runts and the encapsulation errors. On the exam, you may get a question that involves troubleshooting a device and you're going to see an interface statistic screen like this, and then you're going to have to recommend a solution to that problem. For example, if the question asks why the device is operating slowly and you see the connection set to half duplex instead of full duplex, that would be a reason for the slowdown because you effectively cut your bandwidth in half because it's to listen before transmitting. Or if you see a large amount of collisions, but you're running full duplex, that would indicate there's two devices connected to the same switchboard and that is causing you issues. This could be caused by lots of different things such as your cable being improperly run over a fluorescent light or near a power line or something like that. My point is, it's important to be able to read the interface statistics so you can then troubleshoot your network connectivity issues in your routers and switches.```

Here’s a **structural summary** of the lesson on interface statistics:

---

## **1. Introduction to Interface Statistics**
- **Interface**: Physical or logical port on routers, switches, firewalls.
- Each interface generates its own **status** and **statistics** for network performance monitoring.

---

## **2. Key Interface Statistics Covered**

### **2.1 Link State**
- `up/up` = physical connection + protocol operational.
- Indicates cable presence and valid communication protocol.

### **2.2 Interface Info**
- MAC address, IP address.
- **MTU**: Default 1500 bytes (Ethernet).
- **Bandwidth**: e.g., 100 Mbps for Fast Ethernet.
- Used by routing protocols (OSPF, EIGRP) for metric calculation.

### **2.3 Reliability & Load**
- **Reliability**: 255/255 = perfect (no drops).
- **Txload / Rxload**: Transmission/receive busyness (1–255 scale).

### **2.4 Encapsulation & Keepalive**
- **ARPA** = standard Ethernet.
- **Keepalive**: Default 10 seconds.

### **2.5 Duplex & Speed**
- Full/half duplex + bandwidth + media type (e.g., 100BaseTX/FX).

### **2.6 ARP & Timers**
- **ARP timeout**: Default 4 hours.

### **2.7 Queues & Drops**
- **Input queue**: Max size, drops, flushes (SPD for QoS).
- **Output drops**: Zero if link speeds match; positive if congestion.
- **Queuing strategy**: FIFO (default).
- **Output queue size**: Max 40 packets.

### **2.8 Traffic Rates**
- Minute average input/output rates.

### **2.9 Packet Input Statistics**
- Total packets & bytes.
- **Broadcasts**, **runts** (<64 bytes), **giants** (>1518 bytes), **throttles** (buffer failures).

### **2.10 Input Errors**
- **CRC errors**: Failed checksum → packet rejected.
- **Frame**: CRC + non-integer octets.
- **Overrun**: Insufficient hardware buffer.
- **Ignored**: Low internal buffers (noise, broadcast storms).

### **2.11 Special Counters**
- **Watchdog**: Packet >2048 bytes.
- **Dribble condition**: Frame >MTU but <giant (e.g., 1510 bytes).

### **2.12 Packet Output Statistics**
- **Under run**: Sender faster than router can handle.
- **Output errors**: Includes collisions, interface resets.
- **Collisions**: Should be 0 for full duplex.
- **Interface reset**: Since last reboot.

### **2.13 Protocol Drops**
- **Unknown protocol drops**: Unrecognized protocol (e.g., IPX, AppleTalk).

### **2.14 Transmission-Specific Errors**
- **Babbles**: Transmitted frames >1518 bytes (transmit-side giant).
- **Late collisions**: Occur after transmission starts.
- **Deferred**: Waited due to busy media (CSMA/CD).

### **2.15 Carrier & Buffer Issues**
- **Lost carrier / No carrier**: Signal loss.
- **Output buffer failures**: Shortage of shared memory.
- **Buffer swap out**: Packets stored in main memory when queue full.

---

## **3. Exam Relevance**
- **Don’t memorize all** – focus on:
  - Link state
  - Speed & duplex
  - Send/receive traffic stats
  - CRC errors
  - Protocol packet/byte counts
  - Giants, runts, encapsulation errors

- **Troubleshooting examples**:
  - **Half duplex** → slowdown (cuts effective bandwidth).
  - **Collisions in full duplex** → two devices on same switch port.
  - **High CRC errors** → dirty fiber / EMI (e.g., cable near power lines).

---

## **4. Conclusion**
Reading interface statistics is **essential** for troubleshooting connectivity and performance issues on routers and switches.

For example, if you click on the phishing playbook, we can then see that we can open it up and get a 10-page document that tells us exactly what an organization should do in each of the four steps of the NIST incident response process in responding to a phishing attack. This playbook is going to detail how you can automate your responses, how you can detect and analyze it, what actions you take to contain it, eradicate it, and recover from it, and more. In each of these phases, the playbook also has a flow chart that has the relevant actions in it. In the preparation phase, for example, you can see how to determine the core team and their roles, how to review the timeline, how to train your personnel, and the internal and external path to use for that organization. In the detection phase, there's a flow chart that documents the different ways to detect this phishing attack by defining threat indicators. In the analysis phase, the flow chart shows you how to define the risk factors that are involved with the phishing attack, so you can better triage and categorize a phishing attack. In the containment phase, the flow chart also shows different steps used to determine how widespread the attack might be. In the eradication phase, we can see how the report is going to be triaged and confirmed, and then the steps taken to remove any malware that could have been installed during the successful phishing attack. This phase also shows the communications and notifications that could be made based on the severity. In the recovery phase, we see the steps used to recover and remediate the systems. And finally, in the post-incident activity phase, we can see the required steps of conducting the incident review or root cause analysis, the lessons uncovered and applied, together known as the lessons learned, and then the response workflows that are going to be updated based on what we discovered. Now, as you can see, these playbooks are pretty generic, but they do provide you with a great starting point for creating tailored playbooks within your own organization. These playbooks can really help a junior analyst to do their work quickly and more efficiently by following the flowcharts and knowing exactly what to do in response to any given threat. Another great resource in terms of playbooks is the Microsoft provided playbooks on their website. Their playbooks include more technical descriptions of non-automated response activities that you can conduct for a phishing attack, a password spraying attack, or an authentication bypass attack. When it comes to responding to a particular indicator of compromise or incident, you can also automate a lot of these responses for you in a myriad of different ways. To do this, our security operation centers will often implement a SOAR, or security orchestration automation and response system. Now, a SOAR is a class of security tools that helps facilitate incident response, threat hunting, and security configurations by orchestrating and automating runbooks and delivering data enrichment. A SOAR system can be used in incident response to automate many of your response actions by partially or fully automating your playbooks. A SOAR has the capability to scan security and threat data from your systems, analyze it using machine learning, and then automate the process of doing data enrichment to make that data available inside your SIEMs to your analysts. A SOAR can also respond to different threats and incidents by provisioning new resources, creating new accounts, disabling old accounts, starting up new virtual machines, and fully re-imaging a client using automated playbooks. For example, you might have a playbook for a successful phishing campaign that says you need to perform steps one through nine anytime somebody clicks a link in a phishing email. This might include deleting the email from the user's inbox, determining if the other users received that email, isolating workstations from the network that opened the email, conducting a virus scan of those machines, conducting a registry scan of those workstations to confirm infection, backing up the user's data from those machines, re-imaging the workstation, restoring the user's data, and then reconnecting the newly restored workstation to the network. That would be a lot of work to do manually, but by automating this, using a playbook inside of SOAR, I can create what is known as a runbook. Now, a runbook is an automated version of a playbook that can partially or fully automate the incident response process. For example, in the phishing example I just described, we can have the runbook perform the first five steps. Then it can pause and wait for the analyst to confirm the workstation should actually be re-imaged in step five. Then, the runbook can take over again, once the analyst confirms they want that machine re-imaged, and it'll perform steps six through nine. By using these runbooks, we can gain a lot of efficiencies and allow a single analyst to do a lot more work than they could do singly on their own, doing everything manually. This allows us to free up our analysts for higher level work without wasting their time on minor things that could easily be automated. So, what types of playbooks and runbooks should you have in your organization? Well, most organizations face at least three common threats that can be proceduralized using runbooks and playbooks. This includes ransomware, data exfiltration, and social engineering attacks. First, we have ransomware. A ransomware playbook should be used to describe the people, processes, and tools that are going to be employed during a ransomware event. Ransomware playbooks need to also have considerations for determining which systems are impacted, the methods used to impact those systems, how to isolate those systems, and which key stakeholders to work with for different ransomware scenarios based on the data being held for ransom. In general, ransomware playbooks should stress the need to isolate and disconnect networks and systems as quickly as possible to prevent the ransomware from spreading across your network. The system should not be powered off, though. They should only be disconnected because ransomware works through encrypting the data and those encryption keys could be found in the random access memory of that system by a skilled forensic technician if those systems remain powered on during the entire attack. Second, we have data exfiltration. A data exfiltration playbook should be used to describe the specific and necessary tasks that are needed to stop or mitigate ongoing data exfiltration attack, such as notification requirements, the system analysis, and the forensic analysis needed to determine what was accessed and possibly exfiltrated. Forensic analysis can often determine what data was read and what data was transmitted out of the network too. Data exfiltration can be tricky because it can occur from many different types of exploits, including SQL injections, password compromises, and lateral movement across the network into other data stores. Your playbooks and runbooks should always focus on mitigating known instances and protecting the data stores first, then identifying any other potential compromises that may exist in the network. Third, we have social engineering, which usually involves some form of phishing. Now, a phishing playbook should involve the necessary responses to identifying the phishing emails, determining which users clicked on or opened links or files in those emails, and then identifying the extent of the exploitation. Your playbook or runbook may also include a notification to the larger user base to be wary of suspicious emails if your organization is currently being targeted using a spear phishing attack. Now your playbook should focus on identifying all users who have received that email, identifying how many have opened, read, or clicked on the email, and then resetting their passwords and re-imaging their workstations. From an analysis standpoint, you should open the email in a sandbox environment as a form of dynamic analysis in order to determine any IP addresses, URLs, or other indicators of compromise that you can use to identify that phishing campaign once you open it inside the sandbox.```

## **1. Definition & Purpose of Incident Response Playbooks**
- **Playbook**: A checklist of actions to detect/respond to a specific incident type.
- **Purpose**: Ensure documented, repeatable procedures so teams are ready before incidents occur.
- **Usage**: Triage analyst categorizes incident → incident handler follows the relevant playbook.

## **2. Examples of Incident Types Requiring Playbooks**
- DDoS attack, virus, worm, phishing attack, data exfiltration.

## **3. Playbook Structure (using Phishing as an example, aligned with NIST process)**
- **Preparation**: Core team roles, timelines, training, communication paths.
- **Detection**: Threat indicators, detection methods.
- **Analysis**: Risk factors to triage/categorize.
- **Containment**: Assess attack spread.
- **Eradication**: Triage/confirm report, remove malware, communications/notifications.
- **Recovery**: Remediate systems.
- **Post-incident**: Root cause analysis, lessons learned, update workflows.

## **4. SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response)**
- **Definition**: Security tools that automate incident response, threat hunting, and data enrichment.
- **Capabilities**:
  - Scan/analyze security data (with ML).
  - Enrich data for SIEMs.
  - Automate responses (provision resources, create/disable accounts, re-image clients).
- **Runbook**: Automated version of a playbook (partial or full automation).

### **Runbook Example (Phishing)**
Manual steps 1–9 → runbook automates steps 1–5 → pauses for analyst confirmation → automates steps 6–9.

## **5. Common Playbook/Runbook Types by Threat**

| Threat | Playbook Focus |
|--------|----------------|
| **Ransomware** | People/processes/tools; isolate networks (don’t power off—preserve RAM for encryption keys). |
| **Data Exfiltration** | Stop/mitigate exfiltration; notification, system/forensic analysis; protect data stores first. |
| **Social Engineering (Phishing)** | Identify emails & affected users; reset passwords, re-image workstations; sandbox analysis for IOCs (IPs, URLs). |

## **6. Key Takeaways**
- Playbooks are **generic starting points** (e.g., from galleries or Microsoft).
- They help **junior analysts** work quickly/efficiently via flowcharts.
- SOAR + runbooks **free up analysts** for higher-level work by automating routine responses.

In this lesson, we're going to discuss integrations and APIs. Integrations and Application Programming Interfaces, or APIs, as they're commonly called, are the unsung heroes behind the seamless interconnectivity and enhanced capabilities of today's modern software applications and automations. When it comes to automation orchestration, integrations and APIs are really the fundamental elements that are going to drive efficiency, innovation, and scalability in our modern systems. Now, before we dive into the specifics of each of these, let's take a moment to define both an integration and an API. Now, an integration refers to the process of combining different subsystems or components into one comprehensive system to ensure that they can function properly together. An API or Application Programming Interface is a set of rules and protocols that are used for building and integrating application software. An API will allow your product or service to talk to another product or service in a controlled environment and using a specific data exchange format. Now, when we talk about an API, it's a library of programming utilities that are used to enable software developers to access functions or features of another application programmatically. APIs are probably the number one thing that we use in our integrations to be able to communicate between different portions of a microservice or a service oriented architecture. By using an API, we can automate the administration, management, and monitoring of various services and cloud-based infrastructures, as well as a lot of other applications out there. Commonly, our APIs are either going to use REST or SOAP to communicate. REST, or the Representational State Transfer is an architectural style that uses the standard HTTP methods and status codes, uniform resource identifiers, and MIME types to achieve a simple way to interact in a stateless manner with a given web service, REST usually relies on using a JSON formatted message or JavaScript object notation message when it transfers its data, and this makes it a very lightweight protocol that can be easily integrated with existing websites without needing to perform any kind of extensive modifications. Now, SOAP on the other hand stands for Simple Object Access Protocol, and this is a protocol that defines a strict standard with a set structure for each of the messages. And they're usually going to be in XML format and includes a header and a body that's going to be used to transport data between two different services. Now, SOAP is known for being more robust than REST because it has additional security features, and it has the ability to provide transaction compliance. So to sum that up, really what it comes down to is that REST is generally going to be more straightforward and adaptable for you to utilize, but SOAP provides you with higher levels of security and transactional integrity that will cater to some different use cases and requirements in a larger enterprise environment. Now, when I talk about APIs, we need to think about these from the perspective of integration. APIs allow for the integration between lots of different services out there, especially cloud-based services like software as a service or platform as a service. Now, APIs allow us to have a direct integration of different third-party applications into our own web-based applications. By using APIs, we can integrate services together and make function calls to those services instead of having to build the entire service ourself. This is the whole idea of using a service-oriented architecture, also known as microservice architecture, instead of building a single monolithic web application. Now, let me give you an example of how we use integrations and APIs in our business here at Dion Training. So it's really easy for student questions to get missed in that Q&A section if they're expecting us to be able to look for them and answer each of those. Now, in order to overcome this limitation, we would have to be able to rewrite the entire Udemy website to support a ticketing system capability to the instructor backend of their system. So how am I going to get all those Q&A posts loaded into my Freshdesk ticketing system so I can track and answer all of my students without missing any of those questions? Well, if you guess we should use an API, you are absolutely correct. Udemy created an API that allows anybody to programmatically read and respond to any Q&A posts. ## Structural Summary

**1. Core Concepts**
- **Integrations**: Combining subsystems/components into one cohesive system so they work together properly.
- **API (Application Programming Interface)**: Rules/protocols for building and integrating software; enables one product/service to communicate with another in a controlled manner using specific data formats.

**2. API Communication Protocols**
- **REST** (Representational State Transfer)
  - Architectural style using HTTP methods, status codes, URIs, MIME types
  - Stateless, lightweight, typically uses JSON
  - Easy to integrate with existing websites
- **SOAP** (Simple Object Access Protocol)
  - Strict protocol with structured XML messages (header + body)
  - More robust: higher security, transaction compliance
  - Better suited for large enterprise environments

**3. Role of APIs in Automation & Architecture**
- Enable integration between services (especially cloud-based: SaaS, PaaS)
- Allow direct third-party integration into web applications
- Support service-oriented / microservice architectures (vs. monolithic apps)
- Used for provisioning, configuration, management, monitoring

**4. Real-World Example 1: Dion Training Support Integration**
- **Problem**: Student questions on Udemy Q&A (no direct email) were hard to track vs. Freshdesk ticketing system
- **Solution**: Microservice (250 lines Python, AWS Lambda, ~$3 to run every 4 hours)
  - Queries Udemy API for new Q&As → creates tickets in Freshdesk API
  - Reads agent responses from Freshdesk → posts back to Udemy API
- **Result**: Students get answers in original channel; team works from single interface

**5. Real-World Example 2: Lab Integration**
- **Problem**: Students previously needed separate logins and websites for third-party labs
- **Solution**: API integration from learning platform to lab provider
  - Passes student ID, lesson, lab ID, auth token via URL parameters
  - Returns time-limited "magic link" for lab access
- **Result**: Seamless, secure, single-sign-on experience within the course

**6. Key Takeaway**
APIs and integrations create seamless interconnectivity, enhance default capabilities, and are fundamental to driving efficiency, innovation, and scalability in modern automated/orchestrated systems.

In this section of the course, we're going to discuss Documentation and Processes. Now, when we discuss documentation and processes, most of these are going to tie back to a larger concept known as a policy. Now, when I talk about a policy, I'm not specifically talking about technical controls anymore, like adding access control lists to our firewalls and routers, or enabling MAC filtering, or enforcing encryption, and things like that to better secure your network. This is because technical controls aren't the only way for us to secure our network. In fact, a lot of our network protections are going to come in the form of administrative controls, such as policies, and these policies are then documented and translated into processes that our network administrators will follow when they conduct their daily work. Now, policies are one part of a larger concept known as IT governance. IT governance is used to provide us with a comprehensive security management framework for our organizations to build upon. This is done using policies, standards, baselines, guidelines, and procedures. Now, policies are going to be used to define the role of security inside the organization and establishes the desired end state for that security program. This is usually provided by your senior management, and it's going to clarify the level in which the organization will enforce security and how the organization will categorize the controls that are being applied. Policies tend to be very broad, and they provide the basic foundation upon which the standards, baselines, guidelines, and procedures are going to be built. Now, security policies are going to be further divided into three levels. These are organizational, system-specific, and issue-specific. Organizational security policies are going to provide direction and goals. They're going to give you a framework to meet the business goals and define the roles, responsibilities, and terms associated with it. System-specific policies are going to address the security of a specific technology, application, network, or computer system. These system specific policies will tend to be much more technical and they tend to focus on protecting a certain piece of the system or a certain piece of technology. Issue-specific policies are built to address a specific security issue, such as email privacy, employee termination procedures, or other specific issues. As we move beyond policies, we're going to enter the world of standards. Now, standards are going to be used to implement a policy inside of an organization. These include things like mandatory actions, steps, or rules that need to be followed and achieved to be able to get the desired level of security that you want in your network. After standards, we have baselines. And baselines are going to be used as a reference point in our network architecture and design. These baselines are going to be used to document any kind of system, and that way we can go back later and compare it for analysis against the baseline. For example, we may have a baseline configuration for our network switches, and then we can compare the running configuration on any switch to our baseline at any given time to see what changes have been made by our administrators or a possible attacker. Next, we have guidelines. Now, it's important to note that guidelines are not required or mandatory actions, but instead they're simply recommended actions that we should do. Guidelines tend to be very flexible in nature, and they allow for exceptions and allowances when a unique situation occurs. For example, let's pretend I have a guideline that every employee gets 1 terabyte of storage on our cloud servers. Now, that might be fine for most people who work here like our salespeople, or our accountants, or folks like that because they work mostly with text files and those files are small in size. Now, these users are going to have plenty of space with that 1 terabyte of storage limit, but my video editor might come up and say they're running out of space and they need 5 terabytes of storage. ## 1. Definition of Asset Management
- A systematic approach to governing and realizing value from assets over their entire lifecycle.
- Applies to **tangible assets** (buildings, equipment, computers, servers) and **intangible assets** (human capital, IP, goodwill, reputation).
- Involves developing, operating, maintaining, upgrading, and disposing of assets cost-effectively.

## 2. Asset Inventory & Tracking Methods
- **Complete inventory** is the first step.
- **Database systems** (often integrated with configuration management or ticketing systems) automate tracking of:

- **Asset tags** = barcodes or RFID tags with a unique ID for each asset.
- Enables annual inventory scans to verify location and ownership.
- Works best alongside good **change management practices** (notify moves/updates).

## 4. Procurement Lifecycle (Birth to Death)
1. **Change request** – assess impact on business/network.
2. **Procurement** – budget, supplier/vendor selection.
3. **Deployment** – secure configuration, hardened baseline.
4. **Maintenance (Operations)** – monitoring and support (typically 2–5 years).
5. **Disposal** – sanitize data, then reuse, sell, donate, recycle, or destroy.

## 5. Warranty & Licensing
- **Warranty** – track standard and extended warranties in the asset database.
- **Licensing** – track software licenses per asset (e.g., Microsoft Office, specialized video editing software). Ensure licenses match actual usage across devices.

## 6. Assigned Users
- Varies by organization:
  - Some assign multiple devices per user (e.g., unclassified, classified, top-secret computers, phone).
  - Commercial organizations often assign only portable assets (laptops, tablets, phones) to individuals.
  - Shared assets (e.g., call center workstations) may be assigned to a desk or office, not a specific user.
- All assignments should be documented in the asset management database using asset tags/IDs.

In this lesson, we're going to cover IP address management. Now, in our modern enterprise scale networks, it's important that we properly manage our IP addresses efficiently as part of our ongoing processes and procedures. Now, in order to do this at scale, we're usually going to rely on automation and orchestration within the IP address management process. IP address management, also known simply as IPAM or IPAM, is a methodology and suite of tools that's used to plan, track, and manage the IP address space inside of your network infrastructure. Now, whenever you're using a DHCP server on your network, you are already conducting an automated method of assigning and configuring IP addresses to all of your clients. Yes, this is technically IP address management, but it's only one small part of this entire process known as IP address management. Now, when you really think about IP address management, you have to think about all the things that it encompasses, including the comprehensive management of your organization's assigned IP address space, including the tracking, planning, and managing of the network's address inventory. Now, back in the old days, the IP address management functions were usually conducted manually by relying on things like spreadsheets and a whole lot of human intervention. However, with the scale and complexity of modern cloud-based networks, we now have to use automation and orchestration to perform IP address management, 'cause all of our older manual approaches simply cannot operate fast enough to meet our increasingly demanding needs. So instead, we're usually going to be using integrated IP address management inside of our networks by using automation and orchestration functions to transform this process into a dynamic tool that not only oversees the allocation of IP addresses, but also ensures that each device's addresses are going to align with the overall network policies and architectures. By using IP address management, we're going to be able to create a systematic and error-resistant method of managing vast pools of IP addresses inside of our enterprise networks. Now, these automated systems are capable of detecting and resolving IP conflicts, ensuring that two devices are not being assigned the same IP address on that network, and this helps to maintain the integrity of this network. Now, our automated IP address management systems can also be configured to seamlessly interact with our DHCP and DNS servers to provide a more cohesive management of our IP addresses by ensuring that each component is aware of and working in sync with the others on the network. This integration is critically important if you're going to be using horizontal cloud scaling where new virtual machines are being automatically added and removed from your network to support the changing demands from your users. This way, anytime you have new virtual machine that's added into your network, it's automatically going to be assigned a new IP address, and that IP address will also be associated with the host name inside of your organization's internal DNS server too. - **Type**: Legally binding commitment (operational + security priorities).

1. **Prepare / Budget** – gather requirements, plan purchases.

3. **Implement** – purchase, configure, deploy.
4. **Operate & maintain** – daily use + support (≈70% of time).
5. **Optimize** – improve design, reconfigure, add new devices.

### 4. Baselining
- Install network → collect data under normal conditions → **baseline**.
- Use: Compare “normal” vs “current” to identify issues.
- Without a baseline, abnormal cannot be recognized.

### 5. Cable Management
- Document entire cable infrastructure: diagrams, labels, punch‑down blocks, sources/destinations, closet locations.
- **Importance scales with network size**:
  - Small network – hand‑over‑hand tracing is feasible.

- Must be **updated** after every change (new machine, topology change, new vulnerabilities).
- **Contents** include:

  - Network administrator contact info
  - Governing policies
  - Vendor contacts & warranty status

## **1. Introduction to High Availability (HA) & Network Redundancy**
- **Goal:** Maintain continuous operations with minimal downtime.
- **Network redundancy** ensures networks stay up → increases availability.
- **Scope:** Server connections, switch/router links, internet connections.

---

## **2. Redundancy at the Server Level**
- Servers have **2+ network interface cards (NICs)**.
- NICs can operate as:
  - **Active-passive pair** (failover)
  - **Load-balancing group** (shared throughput)
- **Example:** 5 NICs → group 4 together (400 Mbps combined) + 1 standalone backup (100 Mbps).

---

## **3. Redundancy at the Network Device Level**
- Switches/routers with **multiple redundant links**.
- **Example:** Switch with two trunk ports connected to two separate routers → if one router fails, the other takes over.

---

## **4. Three Planning Dimensions for Redundancy**
1. **Device-level** (NICs, cables)
2. **Router & switch paths** (internal network)
3. **External connections** (internet)

---

## **5. High Availability Approaches**

### **A. Active-Active**
- Multiple systems run simultaneously, share load.
- If one fails, others continue (reduced throughput but seamless).
- **Example:** Two 1 Gbps NICs in load-balance → total 2 Gbps; one fails → 1 Gbps remains.

### **B. Active-Passive**
- Standby system idle until primary fails → then takes over.
- Less resource-efficient but reliable fallback.
- **Real-world power example:**
  - *Active-passive:* Diesel generator starts only after grid fails (30–60 sec downtime).
  - *Active-active:* Solar + grid + battery → batteries always feed power; no interruption if one source fails.

### **C. Load Balancers**
- Distribute traffic across multiple servers.
- Monitor server health; reroute traffic from failed nodes.
- Essential for active-active setups.

### **D. Content Delivery Networks (CDNs)**
- Geographically distributed servers.
- Cache content closer to users → lower latency.

Here is a structural summary of the lesson on **Disaster Recovery Metrics**:

## 1. Core Concept
- **Disaster Recovery Metrics**: Quantifiable standards to plan/evaluate an organization's ability to recover IT operations after a disruptive event.
- **Purpose**: Identify organizational risks, measure availability/restoration speed, and support mission-critical operations.

## 2. Availability & Reliability
- **Availability** = Uptime (e.g., % of total minutes operational).
- **"Five nines"** = 99.999% uptime → max 5 minutes downtime/year.
- **"Six nines"** = 99.9999% uptime → max 31 seconds downtime/year.
- **Reliability** = No packet drops + effective data transmission.
- **Key insight**: High availability + high reliability must be balanced to meet business needs.

## 3. Five Key Metrics

| Metric | Acronym | Definition | Ideal Value |
|--------|---------|-------------|--------------|
| Mean Time to Repair | MTTR | Average time to repair a failed device | **Low** (fast repair) |
| Mean Time Between Failures | MTBF | Average time between failures | **High** (longer between failures) |
| Maximum Tolerable Downtime | MTD | Longest inoperable period without irrevocable business failure | Depends on business process |
| Recovery Time Objective | RTO | Time after an event to resume normal operations | As short as feasible (e.g., 0–60 sec) |
| Recovery Point Objective | RPO | Longest tolerable period of lost/unrecoverable data | Short (e.g., ≤6 hours for backups) |

## 4. Examples & Applications
- **MTTR vs. MTBF** (timeline illustration):
  - Time between failure → repair → next failure = MTBF.
  - Time to repair each incident averaged = MTTR.
- **MTD** (Dion Training example):
  - Student support response = 12 hours.
  - Balanced cost vs. speed → teams in US, Philippines, Egypt for geographic diversity.
- **RTO** (power example):
  - Diesel generator → 45–60 sec recovery.
  - Battery backup → 0 sec recovery.
- **RPO** (ransomware example):
  - Backup every 6 hours → 6 hours of potential data loss.

## 5. Final Takeaway
- Balance MTBF (high), MTTR (low), MTD (business-driven), RTO (speed of ops resumption), and RPO (data loss tolerance) to design a cost-effective, resilient disaster recovery plan.

Here is a structural summary of the lesson on redundant site considerations:

## 1. Definition of a Redundant Site
- A backup location/facility that takes over essential functions if the primary site fails.
- Used in Business Continuity Plans (BCP) and Disaster Recovery Plans (DRP).

## 2. Four Main Types of Redundant Sites

| Type | Readiness | Equipment | Cost | Recovery Time |
|------|-----------|-----------|------|----------------|
| **Hot Site** | Fully operational 24/7 | Desks, chairs, computers, phones, network, software | Very high | Instant / near-zero downtime |
| **Warm Site** | Partially ready | Building, power, phones, network; missing computers/phones | Lower than hot | Few days |
| **Cold Site** | Minimal facilities | Empty building, bathrooms, tables/chairs; no network/phones | Cheapest | 1–2 months |
| **Mobile Site** | Portable & configurable | Trailers/tents with power, connectivity, equipment | Varies | Hours to days |

## 3. Key Considerations for Each Type
- **Hot site** – Best for mission-critical functions (e.g., 50 out of 500 employees). Cloud computing makes this easier (AWS, Azure, GCP), but physical office redundancy is still a challenge.
- **Warm site** – Good balance of cost vs. recovery speed. Often used for non-critical staff after a hot site is allocated.
- **Cold site** – Lowest cost, longest recovery. Suitable when downtime of weeks is acceptable.
- **Mobile site** – Fully contained, deployable anywhere (e.g., military DJC2 example). Ideal for disasters in remote or damaged locations.

## 4. Fifth Type: Virtual Site (Cloud-Based)
- **Virtual hot site** – Fully replicated, instantly accessible cloud environment.
- **Virtual warm site** – Partially replicated resources, scalable to full functionality.
- **Virtual cold site** – Critical data/config stored in cloud; resources activated only post-disaster.
- Advantages: Scalability, cost-effectiveness, easy maintenance.

## 5. Platform Diversity
- **Definition** – Using different operating systems, network equipment, or cloud providers across primary and redundant sites.
- **Purpose** – Avoid single point of failure (e.g., a vulnerability affecting Cisco networks won’t take down both sites if the backup uses different gear).
- **Trade-off** – Increased complexity and support costs vs. better resilience.
- **Cloud diversity example** – Multiple cloud providers or different regions within one provider.

## 6. Other Practical Strategies Mentioned
- **Telework + hotel rooms** – As an alternative to full hot sites for employees.
- **Power redundancies** – Solar, batteries, generators, grid.
- **Internet redundancies** – Microwave link, cable, cellular modem backup.
- **Geographic dispersion** – Spread resources across locations for higher redundancy.

## 7. Final Takeaway
- No single solution fits all; organizations often use a **hybrid approach** (different site types for different functions, user groups, or timelines).
- Must consider **people, technology, facilities, and long-term support** – not just tech stack.
- Senior management should be involved in deciding the right mix based on risk, cost, and recovery time objectives.

## **Topic:** Troubleshooting Methodology – Step 1: Identify the Problem

### **Core Objective**
Understand and apply the first step of CompTIA’s troubleshooting methodology: *Identify the Problem*.

### **Key Activities in Step 1**
1. **Gather information from the user**
2. **Identify user changes**
3. **Perform backups before making changes** (if applicable)
4. **Inquire about environmental or infrastructure changes**

---

### **Detailed Breakdown**

#### **A. Understanding the Problem**
- Determine exactly what is wrong, symptoms, and possible causes.
- Clarify vague user statements (e.g., “internet not working” likely means a specific service or site is inaccessible).

#### **B. Questioning the User**
Key questions to ask:
- What happened? What was the status before vs. after the problem?
- Did you see any error messages? Hear unusual noises (e.g., grinding from hard drive)?
- Is anyone else experiencing the same issue? (Helps determine scope: single device vs. network-wide)
- How long has this been happening? (Can link to other changes, like environmental factors)
- Have any recent changes been made? (Configuration, hardware, software, patches, environment)
- What have you already tried to fix it? (Avoid duplicating efforts, e.g., rebooting)

#### **C. Performing Backups**
- **When:** Before any actions in steps 2–6.
- **Why:**  
  - Hardware replacements (e.g., hard drive) can erase data.  
  - Even minor configuration changes may have unintended effects on data.
- **Goal:** Ensure user data is protected before proceeding.

---

### **Key Insight**
> “Things don’t generally just break on their own. Something usually causes it, and that something is a change.”

Identifying the **change** (user-initiated, software, environmental, etc.) is often the key to diagnosing the problem.

Here is a structural summary of the lesson on **Step Two of the CompTIA troubleshooting methodology**:

## I. Core Objective of Step Two
- Establish a **theory of probable cause**
- **Question the obvious**
- Conduct **internal/external research** based on symptoms

## II. Establishing a Theory of Probable Cause
- **Definition**: Guess the problem based on observed symptoms and initial user answers.
- **Information gathered helps determine**:
  - Severity (how many affected, how bad)
  - Investigation focus (hardware, software, OS, application, driver)
- **Probable vs. Possible Cause**:
  - Probable cause = most likely explanation (not unlikely ones like aliens scrambling data)
  - Process: Test most likely → if fails → test next likely → repeat systematically

## III. Questioning the Obvious
- Example: Netflix outage – less likely Netflix servers are down; more likely local internet or device issue.
- Always check simple, common causes first.

## IV. Internal & External Research Based on Symptoms

### A. External Research
- Use sites like **Downdetector** to check if widespread issue exists.
- Use **search engines (Google)** to look up error codes, symptoms, issues.

### B. Physical Inspection
- **Listen**: Fan spinning, clicking/grinding (hard drive), no fan sound.
- **Smell**: Burning smell (processor/motherboard damage).

### C. Reproducing the Problem
- If original symptom gone, try to recreate it.
- Especially important when user has already rebooted or used workarounds.

### D. Internal System Research
- System documentation
- Installation & event logs
- Diagnostic tools

## V. Approaches to Establish a Theory (Using OSI Model)

| Approach | Direction | Description |
|----------|-----------|-------------|
| **Top to Bottom** | Layer 7 → Layer 1 | Start at Application layer, work down to Physical |
| **Bottom Up** | Layer 1 → Layer 7 | Start at Physical (cables), work up to Application |
| **Divide and Conquer** | Start at middle layer (e.g., Layer 3/4) | Test midpoint (e.g., ping 8.8.8.8) → if works, problem is above; if fails, problem is below |

## VI. Leveraging Previous Work
- If other technicians worked on the system:
  - Ask what they already did and touched.
  - Avoid repeating failed fixes.
  - Prevents customer frustration and wasted time.

## VII. Key Takeaway
- Goal of Step Two = **formulate a probable cause theory**.
- Always **question the obvious first**.
- Use **external (internet) and internal (logs, tools) research** when unsure.

Here's a structural summary of the lesson on **Step 3: Test the Theory** (from the CompTIA troubleshooting methodology):

---

## 1. Core Definition (Step 3)
- **Goal:** Test the theory to determine the cause.
- **If confirmed** → Determine next steps to resolve.
- **If not confirmed** → Re-establish a new theory or escalate.

---

## 2. Context Within the Methodology
- **Step 1:** Identify the problem.
- **Step 2:** Establish a probable cause (theory).
- **Step 3:** Test the theory (first time making configuration changes or physical checks).

---

## 3. Example Walkthrough (Computer won’t turn on)
| Theory | Test | Result | Action |
|--------|------|--------|--------|
| Not plugged into wall | Trace cable | Found unplugged → plugged in, still no power | Theory invalid → new theory |
| Wall outlet faulty | Test with volt meter (120V AC, fine) | Not the cause | New theory |
| Power supply faulty | Test/replace PSU | Confirmed | Proceed to fix |

---

## 4. Four Possible Outcomes in Step 3

1. **Theory confirmed** → Fix the problem (repair/replace/config).
2. **Theory not confirmed** → Create new theory (loop back to Step 2 → Step 3 again).
3. **Cause identified but cannot fix** → **Escalate** due to:
   - Lack of authority (e.g., $10k part)
   - Lack of skills (e.g., Windows Server GPO issue)
   - Security issues (e.g., malware, attacker control) → call cybersecurity
4. **Stuck (no theory works)** → **Escalate** to higher support tier.

---

## 5. Escalation & Tiered Support
- **Tier 1:** Basic problems.
- **Tier 2:** More advanced.
- **Tier 3:** Subject matter experts (sysadmins, security, server admins).
- **New technicians** will often need to escalate to Tier 2 or 3.

---

## 6. Key Takeaway
> Step 3 is an iterative loop: guess → test → confirm or retheorize → fix or escalate.

For example, if you're working on the domain controller and you reboot that, this can prevent users from being able to log into their own workstations because the domain controller isn't available to do that authentication. On the other hand, if you're doing something like a file server, this is actually going to disconnect all the users from the file server, but they can still print and they can still log into the servers because the print server and domain controller may still be up. So it's important to understand what is the impact of your particular solution that you're doing as part of your plan of action. Once you have that plan of action in place and you've got the authority to move ahead, you can then implement your solution. This might be installing a new update, replacing a piece of hardware or rebooting a system. Regardless of what it is, you need to make sure you stick with the plan of action you've created and follow the steps that you've outlined because that's what everyone is expecting you to do. If you have a change to that plan, you're going to need to go back and get authorization again, because remember, any changes could implement the larger system and other things across the network that you may not be aware of. ## **Steps 4 & 5 of Troubleshooting Methodology**

### **Step 4: Establish a Plan of Action to Resolve the Problem**
- **Goal:** Determine *how* to solve the probable cause identified (Step 2) and verified (Step 3).
- **Three main approaches:**
  1. **Repair** – Fix the faulty component (e.g., replace a cracked iPad screen).
  2. **Replace** – Swap the entire device if repair is not cost-effective.
  3. **Workaround** – Temporary solution when repair/replacement is too costly or time-consuming (e.g., buying an external monitor while traveling).

- **Key considerations when planning:**
  - **Resources, time, and cost** of the chosen solution.
  - **Impact** on other users/systems.
  - **Authorization** – May need approval from management (e.g., scheduling server reboots during off-hours).
  - **Interdependencies** – Understand how changes to one system (e.g., domain controller, file server) affect others.

### **Step 5: Implement the Solution (or Escalate as Necessary)**
- Execute the plan exactly as outlined and approved.
- If the plan must change, **re‑obtain authorization** before proceeding.
- Always work as part of the larger team and follow organizational policies.

---

**Bottom line:** Plan carefully, weigh repair vs. replace vs. workaround, assess impact, get permission, then execute without deviation unless re‑approved.

## Step 6: Verify Full System Functionality & Implement Preventative Measures (CompTIA Troubleshooting Methodology)

### 1. Core Objective
- Ensure the problem has actually been solved.
- Confirm the system works as well as (or better than) before the issue.

### 2. Verification Actions
- **Check the specific fix**: e.g., new power supply delivers correct voltages (12V, 5V, 3.3V); new RAM is recognized by the OS.
- **Inspect for collateral issues**: Look for accidentally disconnected cables (power, data, fan, LED indicators).
- **Confirm disabled/uninstalled items**: Ensure disabled services stay off after reboot.
- **Review logs & diagnostic tools**: Confirm normal operation.
- **Check updates**: Verify software/drivers have latest security and functional fixes.

### 3. Implement Preventative Measures (If Applicable)
- **Focus on user behavior**: Especially for malware (e.g., warn against downloading from untrusted sites).
- **Physical/environmental changes**: Example – require lidded cups to prevent spills on keyboards.
- **Escalate when needed**: If lacking authority, suggest policy changes to management (especially in large organizations).

### 4. Key Takeaway
- Step 6 ensures resolution **and** reduces recurrence by addressing root causes at the policy or behavior level.

## **Troubleshooting Process (7 Steps)**

### **Step 1: Identify the Problem**
- Gather information by questioning the user
- Identify symptoms (e.g., intermittent connectivity, random drops)
- Ask: *Has anything changed? Can we duplicate the problem?*
- Treat multiple users with similar issues as separate tickets (different root causes possible)

### **Step 2: Establish a Theory of Probable Cause**
- Brainstorm possible causes (faulty router, bandwidth overload, IP conflict, failing switchboard, faulty cable)
- Question the obvious
- Choose an approach: top-to-bottom, bottom-up, or divide & conquer
- *Example for intermittent connectivity:* Start at physical layer (wireless frequency, cabling)

### **Step 3: Test the Theory to Determine the Cause**
- Execute tests to confirm or rule out the theory
- If confirmed → move to Step 4
- If ruled out → return to Step 2 (new theory) → Step 3 again
- *Example cycle:* Test router (logs, reboot) → rule out → test bandwidth (normal) → rule out → test IP conflict (confirmed)

### **Step 4: Establish a Plan of Action & Identify Potential Effects**
- Determine root cause of confirmed issue (e.g., static IP mismanagement, DHCP server problem)
- Plan the fix (e.g., reconfigure DHCP scope)

### **Step 5: Implement the Solution or Escalate**
- If authorized → implement directly
- If not authorized → escalate (e.g., to change advisory board or responsible technicians)

### **Step 6: Verify Full System Functionality & Implement Preventive Measures**
- Confirm the solution works (e.g., proper IP assignment)
- Identify and apply preventive measures (e.g., address unauthorized changes via management)

### **Step 7: Document Findings, Actions, Outcomes & Lessons Learned**
- Record in trouble ticket system (for continuity across shifts)
- Include: symptoms, theories, diagnostic steps/tests, solution, outcome, changes made
- Share lessons via lessons-learned system

---

**Core methodology:** Iterative, methodical progression from identification to documentation, with feedback loops (Step 2 ↔ Step 3) when theories are ruled out.

## 1. Cable Preparation & Connector Attachment
| Tool | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| **Snips / Cutters** | Cut cables from a spool (copper, coax, bundles). |
| **Cable Strippers** | Remove outer jacket to expose inner wires (twisted pair or coax). |
| **Cable Crimpers** | Attach connectors (RJ45/RJ11 for twisted pair; RG6/RG59 for coax). |

---

## 2. Cable Testing & Verification

| Tool | Key Function |
|------|---------------|
| **Cable Tester** | Verifies continuity of all 8 wires in twisted pair cable; checks for breaks and correct pinouts. |
| **Wire Mapping Tool** | Diagnoses specific twisted pair faults: open pair, shorted pair, short between pairs, reverse pair, cross pair, split pair. |
| **Cable Certifier** | Determines cable category (Cat5/6/7/8), throughput, length, delay, resistance; more expensive than basic tester. |
| **Multimeter** | Measures voltage, amperage, resistance; checks for cable breaks (zero ohms = good) and tests power outlets. |

---

## 3. Installation & Identification

| Tool | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| **Punch Down Tool** | Terminates wires on 66/110 blocks or wall jacks; trims excess wire. |
| **Tone Generator (Toner Probe)** | Sends tone on one end (“fox”), detects it audibly on the other (“hound”); traces unlabeled cables in walls. |

---

## 4. Loopback & Reflectometry

| Tool | Application |
|------|-------------|
| **Loopback Adapter** | Connects transmit to receive pins (copper: pin1→pin3, pin2→pin6; fiber: TX to RX). Used with diagnostic software. |
| **TDR (Time-Domain Reflectometer)** | Locates breaks in **copper** cables; estimates distance and severity. |
| **OTDR (Optical TDR)** | Same function for **fiber optic** cables; uses light reflection. |

---

## 5. Fiber-Specific Tools

| Tool | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| **Fiber Light Meter (Optical Power Meter)** | Measures attenuation (loss in dB); uses LED (multimode) or laser (single mode); >0.5 dB loss means clean/polish needed. |
| **Fusion Splicer** | Permanently joins two fiber ends (for long buried runs, not patch cables); requires training. |

---

## 6. Analysis & Monitoring

| Tool | Function |
|------|----------|
| **TAP** | Inline device that copies packets for analysis (security, management); copper or fiber versions. |
| **Spectrum Analyzer** | Measures signal amplitude vs. frequency; used on copper, coax, or RF (e.g., satellite). |

---

## Key Exam Takeaway  
For each cable type (copper twisted pair, coax, fiber) and problem type (break, miswire, attenuation, unknown route, certification), know **which tool** is most appropriate.

- **Use case**: Discover open ports, detect firewalls between sender and target.

## **Ping**
- **Purpose**: Checks connectivity between two devices

### **Windows Usage**
- Default: `ping <domain>` → sends 4 pings
- Custom count: `ping -n <number> <domain>` (e.g., `ping -n 10 jasondion.com`)
- Continuous: `ping -t <domain>` (runs forever)
- Stop continuous: `Ctrl + C`

### **Linux/Unix/OSX Usage**
- Default: runs continuously
- Custom count: `ping -c <number> <domain>` (e.g., `ping -c 4 jasondion.com`)
- Stop continuous: `Ctrl + C`

### **IPv6**
- `ping -6 <domain>` (works same across all OS)

### **Real-world example output**
- Shows packets sent/received, time (ms), average latency

---

## **Traceroute**
- **Command names**: `traceroute` (Unix/Linux/OSX) or `tracert` (Windows)
- **Purpose**: Displays path between source and destination (every hop)

### **How it works**
- Uses Time To Live (TTL) field in IP packet header
- Sends packets with increasing TTL (1, 2, 3...)
- Each router decrements TTL; when TTL=0, packet dropped and ICMP "time exceeded" returned
- Identifies each router/hop along the path

### **IPv6**
- Add `-6` option to traceroute command

### **Common issue**
- Timeout requests (`* * *`) indicate firewall/device not responding to ICMP (security feature)

---

## **Troubleshooting: 4-Step Ping Process**

| Step | Ping Target | If Works | If Fails |
|------|-------------|----------|-----------|
| 1 | `google.com` (or big website) | Connection good → user issue | Go to step 2 |
| 2 | `8.8.8.8` (Google DNS) | Working → DNS issue | Go to step 3 |
| 3 | Default gateway (e.g., 192.168.1.1) | Internet connection issue (modem/ISP) | Go to step 4 |
| 4 | Local client IP (e.g., 192.168.1.23) | Issue between NIC and gateway (cabling/switches) | Ping 127.0.0.1 → if fails, reinstall NIC drivers |

### **Key IP addresses mentioned**
- `8.8.8.8` – Google DNS (high availability, easy to remember)
- `127.0.0.1` – local host (tests NIC/drivers)

---

## **When to use Traceroute**
- When issue is between router and destination
- Identifies where data stops flowing
- Helps locate problematic internal router/firewall for configuration checks

- Default timeout: **21,600 seconds (≈ 6 hours)**.

## 5. **Key Takeaway**
NetStat is a cross-platform diagnostic tool for monitoring active connections, identifying which applications own them, and analyzing network performance statistics.

## 2. **Packet format displayed**
Each packet shows:
- Timestamp
- IP version (IPv4 = `IP`, IPv6 = `IP6`)
- Source IP & port
- Destination IP & port
- TCP flags, sequence number, ACK number, windowing number, options, packet length

- Use `-w` to write to a **PCAP file** (packet capture).
- PCAP files can be reopened in:
  - **Wireshark** (graphical analysis)
  - **tcpdump** again (text-based analysis) using `-r`

---

## 4. **Basic usage examples**
| Action | Command |
|--------|---------|
| Capture live on interface (`en0` on macOS, `eth0` on Linux) | `sudo tcpdump -i en0` |
| Filter by source IP | `sudo tcpdump src 10.128.1.130` |
| Save to file | `sudo tcpdump src 10.128.1.130 -w host130.pcap` |
| Read from file | `sudo tcpdump -r host130.pcap` |
| Filter by source port while reading from file | `sudo tcpdump src port 5475 -r host130.pcap` |
| Show packet contents in hex + ASCII | Add `-x` to any read command |

---

## 5. **Practical considerations**
- Requires **administrative privileges** (to enable promiscuous mode).
- Live capture on a busy network produces too much data to read directly.
- **Filter during collection** → reduces file size, efficient when you know what you’re looking for.
- **Collect everything first, filter later** → useful when indicators of compromise are unknown.

---

## 6. **Relation to exams & further learning**
- Exam doesn’t require deep tcpdump expertise, but you should know:
  - tcpdump and Wireshark are often used together (capture → analyze).
- For more options: `man tcpdump`

---

> tcpdump is a lightweight, text-based packet sniffer, often used with Wireshark. You can filter live traffic or stored PCAP files, and choose to save everything or filter early depending on whether you know what you’re hunting for.

  - Network mapping, documentation, rogue device detection

- **Attacker machine**: Kali Linux (simulating internet/outside)
- **Router**: Separates outside (internet) from inside (target network)
- **Target network**: `10.10.10.0/24`
- **Three target servers**:
  - LAMP-Server (`.10`)
  - Metasploitable2 (`.11`)
  - DVWA (Damn Vulnerable Web App) (`.12`)

## 3. Scanning Steps & Commands

### Step 1: Ping Scan (Host Discovery)
- **Command**: `nmap -sn 10.10.10.0/24`
- **Result**: 4 hosts up (router `.1`, LAMP `.10`, Metasploitable2 `.11`, DVWA `.12`)

### Step 2: SYN Scan for Web Servers (Port 80)
- **Command**: `nmap -sS -p 80 10.10.10.0/24`
- **Result**: Port 80 open on all three servers (closed on router)

### Step 3: SYN Scan on a Single Server (LAMP)
- **Command**: `nmap -sS 10.10.10.10`

### Step 4: Service Version Detection
- **Command**: `nmap -sV 10.10.10.10`
- **Result**: Linux, Apache 2.4.18, Ubuntu (slower scan)

### Step 5: OS Detection
- **Command**: `nmap -O 10.10.10.10`
- **Result**: Linux 3.2 – 4.6

### Step 6: Combined Scan (SYN + Version + OS) on Multiple Targets
- **Command**: `nmap -sS -sV -O 10.10.10.10-12`
- **Duration**: ~140 seconds
- **Results**:
  - **`.10`**: 3 open ports (22, 80, 8080) – Apache 2.4.18, SSH version, Linux 3.2-4.6
  - **`.11`**: 21 open ports (FTP, SSH, Telnet, HTTP, RPC, Samba, etc.) – vulnerable versions: vsftpd 2.3.4, Apache 2.2.8, MySQL 5.0.51, etc.
  - **`.12`**: 1 open port – Apache 2.4.10

## 4. Observations & Notes
- **No DNS** in lab → “unable to determine DNS servers” error (not an issue with IPs).
- **Wide OS version range** due to Docker/container-based virtualization.
- **One unrecognized service** on `.11` (user could submit fingerprint to Nmap).
- **Default scan**: top 1000 ports.
- **Vulnerable versions** identified (e.g., vsftpd 2.3.4) – useful for later exploitation.

## 5. Conclusion
- Nmap provides layered information: alive hosts → open ports → service versions → OS versions.
- Combining flags (`-sS -sV -O`) yields comprehensive reconnaissance data for vulnerability assessment.

When you're dealing with the Cisco Discovery Protocol, it's going to facilitate the collection of detailed device information, including things like model numbers, IP addresses, connected interfaces, and even the device's power consumption. ## **Cable Signaling Issues Overview**
- **Main issues covered:** attenuation, interference, decibel (dB) loss.
- **Context:** wired connections (copper and fiber).

---

### **1. Attenuation**
**Definition:** Loss of signal strength over cable length.

#### **Copper Cables (Twisted Pair, Coaxial)**
- **Cause:** Resistance in copper increases with length → signal weakens.
- **Max distances (standard):**
  - Twisted pair: ~100 meters
  - Coaxial: ~500 meters
- **Other factors affecting attenuation:**
  - Frequency used (higher frequency = higher bandwidth, but more risk of crosstalk)
  - Environmental noise (machinery, power generators)
  - Physical surroundings (temperature, wall construction, insulation)

**Temperature effects:**
- Freezing → brittle, slower signal
- Heat → overheating, melting, fire risk

#### **Solutions for Attenuation**
1. Use proper cable for environment (e.g., shielded twisted pair)
2. Shorten cable length (e.g., 80m limit for twisted pair)
3. Use amplifier/repeater (Layer 1 device) — rebroadcasts signal, resets distance limit

#### **Fiber Cables**
- Same issue but at much longer distances (e.g., single mode fiber ~40 km)
- **Causes in fiber:** cheap cable, dirty connectors (fingerprints block light)
- **Solutions:** higher quality cable, clean/polish connectors

---

### **2. Interference**
**Definition:** Occurs when multiple cables operate in same frequency band in close proximity.

**Prevention methods:**
- Use higher category twisted pair cables (more twists per inch = better resistance to internal interference)
- Avoid running network cables parallel or next to high-power cables

**Best practice:** Plan cable runs away from high-power lines.

---

### **3. Decibel (dB) Loss**
**Definition:** Measurement of signal deterioration.

- **Copper:** dB loss = decrease in voltage
- **Fiber:** dB loss = amount of light lost

**Solutions:**
- **Copper:** higher quality cable, more shielding, more twists per inch
- **Fiber:** higher quality cable (glass > plastic), clean/polish connectors

---

|-------------------|--------------------------------------|
| Attenuation       | Cable certifier (copper), fiber light meter (fiber) |

In this lesson, we're going to discuss interface issues. When we talk about an interface issue, we're really focused on any problems in the network's interface operation that can impact your data transmissions and network performance. These interface issues can significantly affect your network's performance and reliability as well, so it's important to understand how you can best troubleshoot and remediate these different kinds of interface issues. Interface issues include things like increasing interface counters for cyclic redundancy check errors, runts, giants and drops, as well as issues with various port statuses, including the error disabled, administratively down, and suspended port statuses. First, we have increasing interface counters that are associated with cyclic redundancy errors. A cyclical redundancy error or CRC error is any error that occurs when the check of a data's block integrity upon reception doesn't match the check sum value that was attached during the transmission. Now, when this occurs, this indicates that the actual data has been corrupted or altered during the transmission from one device to another. Whenever you see increasing numbers of CRC errors, this can indicate that there is a noise, interference, or other physical issue that's affecting your network connectivity. These CRC errors can occur whenever the frame's check sum doesn't match the check sum that's calculated upon arrival for that data frame. So if you see a high number of CRC errors in your network, this usually is going to indicate that there's an issue related to the electrical interference, cable damage, or a hardware fault inside of your network or your network devices. Second, we have increasing interface counters associated with runts. Now, runts are frames that are smaller than the minimum frame size used by your network. A runt is going to be created whenever there's a collision or other disruption that occurs during your packet transmissions on your network, but they can also be indicative of a deeper network issue that you may need to diagnose and resolve. When I've experienced these type of runts in the past, it's normally going to be caused by a problem like a network card malfunction, using a collision domain that's too large, or simply being a cabling issue that may need your attention. For these reasons, it's essential that you monitor your network traffic to identify and address the root cause of any runt frames that you see in order to maintain the integrity and performance levels associated with your network. Third, we have an increasing interface counter associated with giants. Now, giants are going to refer to any frames that exceed the maximum frame size of your network. A giant is often created due to a misconfiguration or the malfunctioning of a network device. Now, because a giant is so much larger than the expected frame size on your network, a giant can cause network traffic congestion, which can lead to poor performance inside of your networks. To prevent these kinds of congestions, many network devices are going to be configured to simply drop any frames that are larger than the maximum frame size setting for your particular network. If this happens, you're going to see the number of giants increase and the number of drop frames also increase in a direct linear relationship. Like runts, you should always monitor your network traffic to identify and address the root cause of any giant frames that you may find on your network. Fourth, we have the increasing interface counters that are associated with drops. Now, drops occur when the device's buffer is full and it can't accommodate incoming frames or packets anymore. This kind of dropping can lead to the packet simply being discarded by your network device because it's becoming too overloaded or overwhelmed, and therefore it's unable to process any new incoming frames. Now, drops usually occur whenever a high level of network traffic is being experienced by a device, or if the network device is operating beyond its normal operating capacity limits. If you see fairly persistent drop rates inside your network, this will significantly affect the data flow and the network efficiency that you can achieve, so it is important that you set up monitoring to identify and address any underlying issues, such as bandwidth bottlenecks, inefficient traffic management, or to determine if inadequate hardware resources are available. Fifth, we have the issue associated with an error disabled port status. Now, a port status of error disabled is going to be used to indicate that a port on a switch has been automatically shut down by the network system itself because of a network error or a violation in policy. For example, if a port starts to experience a bridge protocol data unit guard violation, that switch can proactively disable the port to prevent possible network loops from occurring. Then it can require that you perform a manual intervention or that you utilize specific configuration commands to re-enable the port for normal operations once more. Six, we have the issues associated with an administratively down port status. Now, an administratively down port status is going to signify that a network port has been intentionally disabled by your network administrators and that the port was not disabled due to some kind of error or network issue. For example, your network administrator may have chosen to shut down a port to perform an upgrade, or to modify the settings on that port. In this type of scenario, the port status will be reflected as administratively down because this indicates that a deliberate, not an error induced deactivation of that port has occurred. Now, to return an administratively down port back to normal operations, again, you simply need to issue a specific command within the network device's interface configuration mode. If you're using a Cisco based device, for example, you're going to use the command no shutdown. to reverse the administrative down status and re-enable the port for normal traffic flow in operations. Before you activate the port using the no shutdown command, you should first ensure that the port is ready to be reactivated and that all the necessary maintenance and configurations have been completed properly to avoid any potential issues once that port is reactivated and back in normal operational use. Seventh and finally, we have the issues associated with a suspended port status. Now, a suspended port status is normally going to indicate when there's a violation of an established protocol or policy within your network. For example, if there is an ether channel misconfiguration on your network switch port, that network switch port will automatically be placed into a suspended port status. Basically, anytime the network determines that a port has the potential to cause a data transmission error or a network loop, that switch port will be put into a suspended port status until the switch port's configuration issue gets resolved and its protocols are realigned. Typically, a suspended port status is going to be used in a port channel configuration whenever a violation of the channeling protocol is going to occur. To solve a suspended port status issue, you need to resolve the underlying configuration issue on that switch port first to be able to ensure it's consistently and correctly configured for ongoing operational use. So, remember, interface issues are defined as any problems in the network's interface operation that could impact your data transmission and network performance. Interface issues include things such as increasing interface counters for cyclic redundancy check errors, runts, giants, and drops, as well as any issues with various port statuses, like the error disabled, administratively down, and suspended port statuses. By learning how to best troubleshoot and remediate the different kinds of interface issues, you can drastically increase the performance and reliability of your networks.```
